nodes.label: James C. Scott
nodes.date_label: The Moral Economy of the Peasant (1976) · Weapons of the Weak (1985) · Everyday Forms of Resistance (1989) · Domination and the Arts of Resistance (1990) · Seeing Like a State (1998) · The Art of Not Being Governed (2009) · Against the Grain (2017)
nodes.description: A political scientist and anthropologist whose agrarian inquiries broaden the evidence used to study domination. The Moral Economy of the Peasant places subsistence and justice in colonial Southeast Asian settings. His everyday-resistance essay asks how dispersed acts can contest appropriation without public organization; intentions matter, and consequences can diverge from them. Domination and the Arts of Resistance distinguishes public performances from less visible criticism, extending beyond the fieldwork behind Weapons of the Weak. In his account of Seeing Like a State, standardization makes intervention possible while imposed designs can suppress the social practices on which they depend; he applies this question to capitalist firms as well as states.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: The Moral Economy of the Peasant (1976); Weapons of the Weak (1985); “Everyday Forms of Resistance” (1989, pp. 33–39 read); Domination and the Arts of Resistance (1990); Seeing Like a State (1998); The Art of Not Being Governed (2009); Against the Grain (2017). Selected book descriptions/metadata, with substantive author accounts in interviews published 2008 and 2015; monographs not newly read in full.
nodes.scope_note: Primary reading in this packet: the 1989 essay, pp. 33–39; the complete Archis interview published in 2008; and pp. 1–3 of West and Plender’s interview, conducted on 12 December 2014 and published in Fall 2015. Monograph bodies remain unread; book dates and their brief descriptions have separate bibliographic/publisher witnesses. Scott’s explanations and historical examples are attributed arguments, not independently verified case histories. Everyday resistance can include violence, and evidence of noncompliance alone does not establish the intentions in his definition. Polanyi is an explicitly acknowledged resource in the 2014 account, but has no individual graph endpoint here. The Thompson relation records specific retrospective reading testimony. Guha’s later foreword credit establishes no influence claim. Later books are selected bibliography, not comprehensive coverage or a career interval.

edges.relationship: Treats dispersed, often concealed acts against appropriation as political practices whose intentions, cooperation and evidential traces need investigation (1989).
edges.evidence_note: Scott’s primary essay, pp. 33–39, especially the definition and qualifications on pp. 36–37. A conceptual resource for studying practice, not a claim that he founded this plural field or that every act of coping is resistance. The definition includes intended claims, symbolic action and outcomes that can backfire; the opening examples also include violence.

edges.relationship: Uses state legibility and the limits of imposed plans to question how comparative accounts join administrative power, standardization and situated social practices (Seeing Like a State, 1998; author explanation, 2008).
edges.evidence_note: Scott’s read Archis interview: first answer on names, addresses and cadastral surveys; global-standardization answer on local counter-planning; free-market question on capitalist firms. The 1998 date has a separate bibliographic witness. This contributes a particular set of comparative questions, not a definition of historical sociology or independent verification of his cases. His extension to firms preserves the argument’s limits as a critique of specified planning practices.

edges.relationship: Scott explicitly identifies The Making of the English Working Class as important to his thinking about class consciousness in a 2014 conversation published in 2015.
edges.evidence_note: West and Plender interview, p. 3, Scott’s answer about intellectual precursors. This is specific acknowledged reading testimony, retrospectively dated to the conversation rather than an invented year of first reading. It does not establish that Thompson supplied every Scott concept or that their different moral-economy arguments are identical. Polanyi’s testimony in the same answer stays in prose because his roster profile is not an individual graph endpoint.

sources.citation: James C. Scott, “Everyday Forms of Resistance,” Copenhagen Papers / The Copenhagen Journal of Asian Studies 4 (1989): 33–62, DOI 10.22439/cjas.v4i1.1765.

verification.note: Read primary pp. 33–39 in the journal-hosted 30-page PDF, https://rauli.cbs.dk/index.php/cjas/article/download/1765/1785/. The opening discusses actions absent from conventional public records; pp. 36–37 define resistance through intended claims on appropriation and recognize symbolic action and unintended outcomes; pp. 38–39 discuss poaching, property and tacit cooperation. The examples include violent acts, so everyday does not mean invariably nonviolent. The rest of the article was not read substantively; notes on the final pages were inspected only as references. The journal page supplies 1989-05-05; the event retains year precision. Scott’s historical examples and authors he quotes were not independently verified.

rationale: The additions answer concrete missing method/work coverage, not citation rank or absence of standalone nodes alone. Scott’s read 1989 essay and two author interviews distinguish intentional everyday resistance, hidden/public performance and state legibility; one direct retrospective testimony supports the Thompson arrow. Lefebvre’s read 1974 primary introduction supplies a bounded production-of-space resource, with French publication, journal extraction and credited English translation kept distinct. Existing field prose, old chronology events, source qualifiers and coverage metadata remain exact. No OpenAlex investigation, identity merges, automatic dissertation links, career intervals, endpoint repairs or claims of whole-monograph reading.

strand.title: Everyday resistance and the limits of public evidence
strand.focus: Scott’s 1989 essay treats intended efforts against appropriation as political action, including dispersed and concealed acts. Reading them requires attention to cooperation, symbols and the danger of misidentifying motives or outcomes. His categories are a distinct resource, not a synthesis of Bourdieu’s and de Certeau’s projects.

strand.title: State legibility and the limits of imposed plans
strand.focus: Scott asks how names, addresses, surveys and standards make societies open to administrative intervention, and how planning is altered by the social practices it encounters. His 2008 account also applies standardization to capitalist firms. These are comparative questions with attributed examples, not a single theory of every state.
strand.works: Seeing Like a State (1998); “Seeing Like a Society,” author interview (2008)

strand.title: Producing space through social practice and power
strand.focus: Lefebvre’s 1974 introduction asks how spaces and their codes are produced and changed through social practices, planning and power. Space participates in these relations rather than merely containing them. This is his theoretical proposal; the excerpt neither supplies a GIS procedure nor establishes a uniform school of spatial historians.
strand.works: La production de l’espace (1974), introduction excerpt pp. 19–27; The Production of Space, trans. Donald Nicholson-Smith (1991, metadata only)
